In OPPENHEIMER FUND, INC. v. SANDERS, 437 U.S. 340, 98 S.Ct. 2380, 57 L.Ed.2d 253 (1978), the Court held that Rule 23
authorized a district court “to order one of the parties to perform the tasks necessary to send notice,” and that Eisen did not foreclose
apportioning some of the costs of those tasks to defendant as part of the court’s order. The Court admonished that “courts must not stray
too far from the principle underlying [Eisen] that the representative plaintiff should bear all costs relating to the sending of notice because
it is he who seeks to maintain the suit as a class action.” Id. at 359, 98 S.Ct. at 2393, 57 L.Ed.2d at 270. However, the Court made clear
that in some circumstances, the cost of carrying out the task will be so insubstantial as to make it administratively inconvenient to shift
the charge to plaintiff; moreover, some tasks are carried out by defendant “in any event in the ordinary course of its business” and the
expense should not be shifted to plaintiff. In Oppenheimer Fund, the information requested was contained in documents in the hands of a
third-party transfer agent, and the representative party was required to pay the costs of extracting the information from the documents.
Relying on Oppenheimer Fund, the Third Circuit in Larson v. AT&T Mobility LLC, 687 F.3d 109 (3d Cir. 2012), held it was an
abuse of discretion for the district court to refuse to order defendant-Sprint to run a computer search of its billing records to help identify
class members:
* * * Sprint has acknowledged here that the database search * * * “could result in the identification of millions of Settlement
Class Members.” * * * The cost of identifying those “millions” of class members is approximately $100,000. If only two million
people were identified through that billing records search, the search would have cost approximately 5 cents per class member
identified in 2009. Including the expense of mailing the individual notice, the cost would have been approximately 43 cents per
class member. Given the size of the class and the due process rights at stake, these are not troublingly high sums.
* * *
* * * [W]e fail to see why running those search inquiries is unreasonable, and no explanation for that conclusion was provided
